It unequivocally concludes that the drug robustly reduces vertebral fracture risk during active treatment.

report:
## Yes — Denosumab Reduces Vertebral Fracture Risk in Osteoporosis

**The evidence strongly supports this conclusion.** The pivotal randomized, placebo-controlled FREEDOM trial (published in *NEJM*, 2009) found that in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, denosumab given subcutaneously every 6 months for 36 months significantly reduced the risk of vertebral fractures. Specifically, new radiographic vertebral fractures occurred in 2.3% of denosumab-treated subjects versus 7.2% of placebo-treated subjects — a 68% relative risk reduction (p<0.001), with an absolute risk reduction of about 4.8%. Denosumab also reduced nonvertebral and hip fracture risk in this trial ([nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493); [panoramaortho.com](https://www.panoramaortho.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/Denosumab-for-Prevention-of-Fractures-in-Postmenopausal-Women-with-Osteoporosis.pdf)).

This benefit has proven durable: the 10-year FREEDOM Extension study showed sustained low rates of vertebral fracture and continued reduction in nonvertebral fracture risk with long-term continuous treatment, without increased infection, cancer, or immunogenicity risk ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/PMC8799550](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8799550/)).

**An important caveat:** the antifracture benefit is contingent on continued treatment. Discontinuing denosumab causes a rebound increase in bone turnover and rapid loss of BMD gains, which is associated with an increased risk of multiple vertebral fractures — sometimes exceeding pretreatment baseline risk. Post hoc analysis of the FREEDOM trial and its extension specifically documented this rebound phenomenon ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/PMC3617467](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3617467/)).

**Bottom line:** Denosumab robustly reduces vertebral fracture risk in osteoporosis during active treatment, supported by high-quality RCT and long-term extension data, but patients who stop the drug should transition promptly to alternative antiresorptive therapy to avoid rebound fracture risk.
